concepts.name: Open-loop versus closed-loop control
concepts.summary: Explain how feedback from a measured output corrects errors, in contrast to open-loop control that applies inputs without measuring the result.

concepts.name: Plant, controller, sensor, actuator
concepts.summary: Identify the roles of each element in a feedback loop and name the reference, error, control and output signals.

concepts.name: Block diagram elements
concepts.summary: Read block diagrams with blocks, summing junctions and pickoff points and describe the signal flow they represent.

concepts.name: Transfer function of a plant
concepts.summary: Understand a transfer function as the ratio of output to input Laplace transforms with zero initial conditions.

concepts.name: Poles and zeros of a transfer function
concepts.summary: Define poles and zeros as roots of the denominator and numerator and locate them on the s-plane.

concepts.name: Step response features
concepts.summary: Describe rise time, peak overshoot, settling time and steady-state value on a step response plot.

concepts.name: Stability as bounded response
concepts.summary: Explain that a stable system's response to bounded inputs stays bounded and decays to equilibrium when disturbed.

misconceptions.text: Feedback control always makes a system faster and more stable.
A transfer function describes the system's response to one specific input such as a step.
Overshoot and rise time are the same thing, both describing how quickly the output reaches the target.

concepts.name: Block diagram reduction
concepts.summary: Simplify block diagrams with series, parallel and feedback rules to obtain closed-loop transfer functions such as G/(1+GH).

concepts.name: First-order time constant and DC gain
concepts.summary: Compute time constant and DC gain from a first-order transfer function and predict its step response.

concepts.name: Damping ratio and natural frequency
concepts.summary: Use damping ratio and natural frequency to classify underdamped, critically damped and overdamped responses and estimate overshoot and settling time.

concepts.name: Pole location and response
concepts.summary: Relate pole positions in the s-plane to decay rate, oscillation frequency and stability of the time response.

concepts.name: Routh-Hurwitz stability test
concepts.summary: Build a Routh array from a characteristic polynomial to count right-half-plane roots and find gain ranges for stability.

concepts.name: Steady-state error and system type
concepts.summary: Apply the final value theorem and error constants to compute steady-state error for step, ramp and parabolic inputs by system type.

concepts.name: Proportional gain effect on closed-loop poles
concepts.summary: Predict how raising proportional gain moves closed-loop poles and changes speed, overshoot and steady-state error of a simple loop.

misconceptions.text: Increasing proportional gain indefinitely improves performance without any downside.
Steady-state error can be found only by simulating the response, not analytically.
A system with all poles in the left half-plane has no overshoot.

concepts.name: Root locus construction rules
concepts.summary: Sketch a root locus using branches, real-axis segments, asymptotes, breakaway points and angles of departure.

concepts.name: Root locus gain selection
concepts.summary: Analyse the locus to choose a gain that meets damping and settling targets and recognise when no gain can.

concepts.name: PID controller terms
concepts.summary: Apply P, I and D actions and predict how each affects rise time, overshoot, settling and steady-state error.

concepts.name: Frequency response and Bode plots
concepts.summary: Construct and read asymptotic Bode magnitude and phase plots from a transfer function.

concepts.name: Gain and phase margins
concepts.summary: Determine gain and phase margins from Bode plots and relate them to closed-loop stability and damping.

concepts.name: Nyquist stability criterion
concepts.summary: Use encirclements of -1 by the Nyquist plot and open-loop RHP poles to determine closed-loop stability.

concepts.name: PID tuning heuristics
concepts.summary: Tune PID gains using Ziegler-Nichols rules or manual iteration and judge the resulting response.

concepts.name: Sensitivity and disturbance rejection
concepts.summary: Analyse sensitivity and complementary sensitivity to explain disturbance rejection and noise tradeoffs.

misconceptions.text: Derivative action improves any loop and is safe with noisy measurements.
Positive gain and phase margins computed from the Bode plot guarantee stability for any plant.
Ziegler-Nichols tuning yields optimal, well-damped responses.

concepts.name: Lead compensator design
concepts.summary: Design a lead compensator to add phase near crossover and improve transient response and margins.

concepts.name: Lag compensator design
concepts.summary: Design a lag compensator to raise low-frequency gain and reduce steady-state error without disturbing crossover phase.

concepts.name: Loop shaping
concepts.summary: Shape the open-loop frequency response to meet bandwidth, margin, tracking and noise specifications together.

concepts.name: Fundamental performance limitations
concepts.summary: Evaluate how right-half-plane zeros, delays and the waterfall effect limit achievable bandwidth and sensitivity.

concepts.name: Integrator windup and anti-windup
concepts.summary: Diagnose windup under actuator saturation and select anti-windup schemes such as clamping or back-calculation.

concepts.name: PID derivative filtering and setpoint weighting
concepts.summary: Implement PID with derivative filtering and setpoint weighting while analysing their effects on noise amplification and setpoint response.

concepts.name: Time delay in feedback loops
concepts.summary: Analyse the phase penalty of delay and apply Pade approximation or Smith-predictor ideas to loop design.

concepts.name: Two-degree-of-freedom control
concepts.summary: Separate tracking from disturbance rejection using prefilters or feedforward and justify the structure chosen.

misconceptions.text: A lead compensator can be made arbitrarily strong to gain unlimited phase and bandwidth.
Anti-windup is only needed if the integral gain is too high.
Right-half-plane zeros can be cancelled by placing a pole at the same location in the controller.

concepts.name: Linearisation validity and gain scheduling
concepts.summary: Assess when linearised models are valid and design schedules or alternatives when nonlinearity breaks the assumptions.

concepts.name: Cascade and multi-loop architecture design
concepts.summary: Create cascade and multi-loop architectures with inner and outer loops suited to a plant's structure and time-scale separation.

concepts.name: Model identification for design
concepts.summary: Develop plant models from experimental frequency or step data and quantify uncertainty for controller design.

concepts.name: Robust stability and uncertainty
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a design remains stable under modelled plant uncertainty using the small gain theorem and sensitivity bounds.

concepts.name: Conflicting specification prioritisation
concepts.summary: Critique conflicting requirements on speed, robustness, noise, actuator effort and cost, and justify prioritisation.

concepts.name: Sampling and computation delay effects on margins
concepts.summary: Evaluate how sampling, quantisation and computation delay erode margins and choose discretisation methods and rates.

concepts.name: Controller validation and commissioning
concepts.summary: Create simulation and hardware test plans, including margin measurement and worst-case cases, to verify and tune a deployed loop.

misconceptions.text: A controller that works well in simulation will work on the real plant if the nominal margins are good.
Sampling at just above twice the bandwidth is enough for digital control.
A single linear model identified at one operating point suffices across the whole range.
